newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile police raid German enclave, search for chief.
newsitem.headline: Chile police raid German enclave, search for chief.

text.p: Police on motorcycles, trucks and horseback raided a secretive German colony in Chile on Wednesday seeking to arrest its fugitive leader, Paul Schaefer, who faces charges of sexually abusing children.

More than 200 police pushed into the heavily guarded enclave known as Colonia Dignidad (Dignity Colony) in a long convoy of buses, trucks and ambulances following the arrest of two of Schaefer's lieutenants on Tuesday night.

"This is a raid and the objective is the arrest of Paul Schaefer," police spokesman Raul Toro said. The sweep "will last as long as it takes to carry out the order" for Schaefer's arrest, issued last year by investigating judge Hernan Gonzalez, Toro added.

Police wearing bulletproof vests met no armed resistance at the electrified, barbed-wire gates to the colony, sprawling across fields and valleys in the Andean foothills near the town of Parral, 200 miles (320 km) south of Santiago.
A police helicopter circled overhead while loudspeakers in the village blasted the sound of church bells. Officers on horseback patrolled the surrounding wooded hills.

The raid followed a series of police inspections at the colony since May and a cryptic report of a sighting of Schaefer at an Argentine ski resort last weekend, which Chilean officials later said was a diversionary ploy.

It was the boldest police action yet against the 36-year-old colony, once protected by Chile's military rulers, where settlers came from Germany in the early 1960s to live in secrecy amid scenic farms and traditional Bavarian homes.

Schaefer, a corporal in the Nazi army in the Second World War and now in his late 70s, was believed to be holed up somewhere in the colony although settlers say they have not seen him for about eight months. Officials vowed to find him.
"Schaefer will be detained sooner rather than later," Deputy Interior Minister Belisario Velasco said, adding that officials believed settlers might have unregistered weapons.

There were few witnesses to the raid because police apparently waited until dozens of journalists posted outside the colony's gates since May had left. Pictures televised later on a private station showed police with dogs inspecting tunnels and hallways and no obvious signs of resistance.
"The idea is to find the person we're looking for and to bring justice, because in the end justice will be imposed," President Eduardo Frei's top political adviser, Juan Villarzu, said.
Colony members say they fear that Schaefer, charged with molesting at least five Chilean boys at a settlement boarding school, would commit suicide rather than be arrested.

A former Protestant preacher and charismatic speaker, he has been accused of molesting boys at Colonia Dignidad since at least 1966. Media reports say he fled Germany in about 1957 after charges of fondling youngsters at an orphanage he founded in Bonn.
Colonia Dignidad's leaders also face charges of illegal detention of children, obstruction of justice and tax evasion.

The new child molestation charges, filed last year, have galvanised opposition to the colony inside Frei's government and alienated the settlement's one-time supporters among the right-wing and the military.
Police late on Tuesday arrested two members of the colony on charges they refused to appear in court to give evidence against Schaefer. A third German was arrested early Wednesday.
